title: ‘StarCraft 3,’ an Open-World Shooter Game, Coming in 2030; First Look Revealed
description:
A new “StarCraft” game is coming from Blizzard Entertainment in 2030.

	While technically “StarCraft 3,” the game, an open-world shooter, will be ti
body:
A new “StarCraft” game is coming from Blizzard Entertainment in 2030.

	While technically “StarCraft 3,” the game, an open-world shooter, will be titled “StarCraft.”

	The new installment will mark the first mainline title in video game franchise since “StarCraft II: Legacy of the Void” debuted in 2015. The original “StarCraft” launched in 1998.

	The “StarCraft” news was announced Saturday during BlizzCon 2026 (the first edition of the Blizzard fan-festival event hosted since 2023) at the Anaheim Convention Center. Also revealed at the BlizzCon opening ceremony was an animated TV series adaptation of Blizzard Entertainment’s popular “Diablo” video game franchise that is currently in development at Netflix.
	

	Variety will be on the ground at BlizzCon Sept. 12-13 and readers can follow along with our coverage of the event here.

	Watch the first teaser for the new “StarCraft” game in the video below.

title: Inside ‘Ah Girl,’ the Singapore Drama Built From a Director’s Own Childhood: ‘We Can’t Fly Without First Learning How to Walk’
description:
Ang Geck Geck Priscilla spent more than a decade making “Ah Girl” before she ever made “Ah Girl.”

	Three short films and a decade of festival labs
body:
Ang Geck Geck Priscilla spent more than a decade making “Ah Girl” before she ever made “Ah Girl.”

	Three short films and a decade of festival labs later, the Singaporean director’s feature debut is a Centrepiece selection at the Toronto Film Festival for its North American premiere, following wins at Rotterdam and Hong Kong.

	The character first appeared in Ang’s 2013 short “Broken Crayon,” which won best short film at the Singapore Short Film Festival that year and kicked off a trilogy that continued with “Little Pigs” and “Happy Birthday.” 
	

	Ang says she had a feature in mind from the beginning but didn’t feel ready to commit to one. “A feature is a much bigger commitment, creatively, financially and emotionally, and I wanted to make sure I was ready for that responsibility,” she says. The shorts became a testing ground for her instincts as a director. “We can’t fly without first learning how to walk,” she says. “The short films were me learning how to walk. ‘Ah Girl’ is the film I was preparing myself to make all along.”


	Writing from a child’s vantage point meant deliberately withholding adult understanding rather than supplying it. Ang says she kept returning to a single question while drafting the script: what does Ah Girl see, feel and think is happening, rather than what the audience needs to be told. Children, she says, register far more than the adults around them assume. “She is absorbing everything,” Ang says of her protagonist. “I want the adults watching the film to try to understand the child.”

	That dynamic sharpens around the film’s central dilemma, in which Ah Girl is asked to choose which parent she wants to live with. “Sometimes they are hoping to hear the answer that will make them feel better about themselves,” she says. “A seven-year-old should never have to carry that emotional responsibility.” She adds that the film returns throughout to the gap between listening to a child and making a child responsible for an adult’s decision: “The adults keep asking her what she wants, but very few of them actually stop to ask what she needs.”
	

	The 1990s setting is deliberate rather than nostalgic, Ang says, tied to the absence of a phone or a message as an escape hatch when a parent walks away. “That distance creates a certain helplessness and desperation,” she says. Casting took close to a year, resolving in newcomer Ong Xuan Jing, who spent three months building trust and playing games with Ang before filming began rather than rehearsing lines. “I wasn’t necessarily looking for the best child actor,” Ang says. “I was looking for someone who was already close to Ah Girl as a person.”

	Ang also resisted turning either parent into a villain, even as the film shows both failing their children in different ways. “They are two people who became parents before they were emotionally ready to be parents,” she says. “Loving your child and knowing how to love your child are not always the same thing.”

	“Ah Girl” was developed at Southeast Asia Fiction Film Lab, where it won the Open SEA Fund Award, and went through Golden Horse Film Project Promotion’s work-in-progress section, the Hong Kong-Asia Film Financing Forum and Focus Asia at the Far East Film Festival in Udine. 

	Aggregate Films, IFA Media and Kusu Films are credited as producers, alongside Charlyn Ng and Wendy Lie, and the project was backed by Infocomm Media Development Authority Singapore’s New SG Director Grant and the Purin Film Fund. Hoping Chen, who won the best film editing award for “Bel Ami” at the 61st Golden Horse Film Festival, edited the film.

	Since premiering at the International Film Festival Rotterdam, where it won the Youth Jury Award, “Ah Girl” has traveled to Melbourne, Hong Kong, Udine, Innsbruck, Shanghai, Munich, Da Nang, Bucheon and Malaysia. 

	The film also collected a Golden Firebird Award for best actress in a Chinese-language film at the Hong Kong International Film Festival, along with a best actress prize and the New Hope Award at the Malaysia International Film Festival. Ang says she’s been struck by how audiences across very different cultures have told her they see themselves in Ah Girl. “There is something very powerful about two strangers not sharing the same language or upbringing, but recognizing the same emotion in each other,” she says.

	Ang isn’t finished with the character. She hopes to follow Ah Girl through a trilogy spanning childhood, adolescence and middle age, ideally with the same cast aging alongside their roles. Before that, though, she’s turning to a psychological horror feature expanded from “Broken Crayon,” the thesis short that started it all. “I’ve loved horror films since I was about six years old, so it’s actually quite funny that after all these years, I’ve never made one,” she says. “So no, Ah Girl hasn’t left me. I’m just letting her grow up a little while I go and scare some people first.”

schema.headline: Inside ‘Ah Girl,’ the Singapore Drama Built From a Director’s Own Childhood: ‘We Can’t Fly Without First Learning How to Walk’

title: ‘The Odyssey’ Becomes Universal’s Highest-Grossing Film of All Time
description: On a box office voyage for less than two months, Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” has become the highest-grossing film in the history of Universal
body:
On a box office voyage for less than two months, Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” has become the highest-grossing film in the history of Universal Pictures.

	The 114-year-old film company announced the milestone on Saturday, when the Matt Damon-led epic’s weekend haul will bring its domestic earnings to $601.2 million, with an international tally of $1.083 billion in ticket sales. That’s a grand total of $1.68 billion worldwide, with a slew of records set along the way.
	

	“What Chris and Emma [Thomas] have created will go down as one of the most ambitious and brilliantly executed films in cinematic history. A generational event that galvanizes moviegoing itself,” said Donna Langley, chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment.


	Nolan’s meticulously hand-crafted movie, shot across the globe and starring some of the biggest names in Hollywood, recently reclaimed the top box office position in its eighth weekend in theaters. The project represents the biggest opening of Nolan’s career, ahead of “The Dark Knight Rises,” the first comic book adaptation to gross $1 billion (and the first for studio Warner Bros.) “The Odyssey” is now the Oscar winner’s highest-grossing film ever. It was produced by Thomas and Nolan via their Syncopy banner, with executive producer Thomas Hayslip.  

	More superlatives: “The Odyssey” is the top-grossing R-rated film in history, as well as the biggest earner ever for IMAX. While based on 3,000-year-old IP, the movie is the first non-sequel film to gross over $1 billion overseas since 2009.

	It’s not just an undeniable victory for Nolan. Earlier this summer, Variety reported about the legacy marker “The Odyssey” represents for Langley. She brought Nolan into the Uni fold after his decisive departure from Warner Bros. in 2021, paving the way for the best picture winner “Oppenheimer” and, now, the best picture hopeful “Odyssey.”
	

	This weekend’s numbers further cement Universal’s box office dominance in 2026, leading all studios with 26% of the market share and grossing nearly $5 billion to date in 2026. The studio is the first to cross $4 billion at the global box office this year and the first to cross $3 billion at the international box office.

title: Jeremy Thomas Remembered as a Filmmaker ‘Full of Stories’ and a ‘Rebel With Taste’: ‘The Canon of His Work Is Unmatched’
description: Tributes have begun flowing from across the film world for Jeremy Thomas, the legendary British producer who passed away on Friday at the age of 77.
body:
Tributes have begun flowing from across the film world for Jeremy Thomas, the legendary British producer who passed away on Friday at the age of 77.

	“He made great movies and was a loyal, dear friend,” said producer and publisher Charles Finch. “His father, Ralph, made a film with my father, Peter, called ‘No Love for Johnnie.’ We spent plenty of time talking movies, cars and praising the devilled kidneys as Wilton’s.”


	Luca Guadagnino, who recently put Thomas on camera for his Venice-bowing documentary “Joie De Vivre” to talk about Italian director Bernardo Bertolucci (with whom he made five films), offered Variety a statement about the producer.
	

	“Jeremy Thomas’ death leaves a gigantic void. The space he was fulfilling was a space of pure cinema. Someone who knew how to collaborate with filmmakers and make them better, and how to be himself — a great filmmaker,” he said. “The canon of his work is unmatched, and some of the greatest movies of the past 50 years have been produced by him. And the level of the partnerships that he established in his career is incredible, from Nagisa Oshima to Bernardo Bertolucci. He was a generous man. He was a kind man. He was a man full of stories to tell, but at the same time, very curious to hear others people’s stories. I regret not having been able, in my life, to be produced by the great Jeremy Thomas, and I say a very moved goodbye to him.”

	Thomas was greatly admired and loved by fellow British producers, such as Danny Boyle’s producing partner Andrew Macdonald. Macdonald told Variety that “Jeremy and I bonded over his father and my grandfather both producing films for Rank in the 1950s. He was a hero for me. A rebel with taste.”  Macdonald’s grandfather was Emeric Pressburger, the co-writer, co-director and producer of “The Red Shoes” and “Black Narcissus,” among other classics.
	

	On social media, Edinburgh Film Festival CEO and director Paul Ridd said that the “loss of Jeremy Thomas is enormous, to film culture and to the world,” adding that he was “such a beautiful man and a extraordinarily generous supporter” of the festival. 

	Adrian Wootton, chief executive of Film London and the British Film Commission, said that Thomas’ passing was, “Such terribly sad news for Jeremy’s loved ones, family, friends, colleagues, the filmmakers and for the British Film Industry he did so much for.”

	Across a career spanning more than half a century, Thomas produced 80 features, championing the work of both international cinema and daring auteur filmmakers in the process. In 1988 he won the best picture Oscar for Bertolucci’s “The Last Emperor.”

schema.headline: Jeremy Thomas Remembered as a Filmmaker ‘Full of Stories’ and a ‘Rebel With Taste’: ‘The Canon of His Work Is Unmatched’

title: Venice Film Festival Reveals Award Winners (Updating Live)
description:
The Venice Film Festival is about to reveal its award winners, including the prestigious Golden Lion for best film. 

	Last year, Jim Jarmusch took
body:
The Venice Film Festival is about to reveal its award winners, including the prestigious Golden Lion for best film. 

	Last year, Jim Jarmusch took home the top prize for his family triptych “Father Mother Sister Brother,” while Benny Safdie won the Silver Lion for best director for his Dwayne Johnson-led “The Smashing Machine” and Kaouther Ben Hania’s Gaza drama “The Voice of Hind Rajab” was awarded the grand jury prize. 


	Ben Hania is serving on this year’s competition jury, which is headed by president Maggie Gyllenhaal. Other jury members include Hong Kong filmmaking giant Johnnie To, Afghan filmmaker Shahrbanoo Sadat, French director and screenwriter Xavier Giannoli, “The Brutalist” composer Daniel Blumberg and U.S.-based Italian film academic Francesco Casetti.
	

	Films in the running for the Golden Lion include Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime,” Danny Boyle’s “Ink,” Casey Affleck’s “Company,” Werner Herzog’s “Bucking Fastard,” Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s “NAZA,” Hirokazu Kore-eda’s “Look Back,” Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” Florian Zeller’s “Bunker” and more.

	Throughout the ceremony, several took a moment to remember Oscar-winning British producer Jeremy Thomas, who died on Friday at the age of 77.

	Gianluca Farinelli, head of Italy’s Bologna Film Archives and artistic director of Italy’s David di Donatello Awards, said:  “He loved cinema; cinema made by humans and not by AI. He deeply loved our country. He produced masterpieces, also by great Italian directors.”

	Thomas won a best picture Oscar for Bernardo Bertolucci’s “The Last Emperor” in 1988, one of nine Academy Awards for the film. He would make five features across 17 years with the Italian director.
	

	Added Italian actor and producer Riccardo Scamarcio, who won the Horizons best actor prize for “The Children of the “Monkey”: “Jeremy, a great man of cinema. I salute you, my friend!”

title: Kling AI’s TIFF Market Panel Illuminates Tech Challenges and Human-Led Solutions in AI Filmmaking: ‘The Script Is Still the Blueprint’
description: Kling AI hit the opening morning of the inaugural TIFF: The Market with a lively, well attended panel, “A New Creative Paradigm: Consistent, Cinemat
body:
Kling AI hit the opening morning of the inaugural TIFF: The Market with a lively, well attended panel, “A New Creative Paradigm: Consistent, Cinematic AI Video Powered by Kling AI,” geared towards a Canadian industry audience of animation and live-action film creators eager for up-to-date insight into their roles and human skills in rapidly evolving production workflows.

	The panel, moderated by Tony Pu, Kling AI’s head of creator community and industry partnerships, Europe and North America, continued the discussion started at Kling AI’s Cannes Film Market session, where the company announced it had signed on as exclusive global technological brand partner on Evolutionary Films’ animated feature “Minibots.”
	

	Direct from the frontlines, “Minibots” producer and co-founder of Evolutionary Films Diane Shorthouse and AI filmmaker and founder of Amissa Studios Issa Sissoko (who has worked and consulted for the likes of Antoine Fuqua, Darren Aronofsky, and Doug Liman) discussed the practical realities of AI-assisted filmmaking with a focus on existential aspects of the work. Both panelists and their teams utilize tools from Kling AI’s AI creative productivity platform.


	The fundamental job of a producer is still to serve the director’s creative vision, Shorthouse said, but the tools are different.

	“The script is still the blueprint, so I’m not thinking about prompts, I’m thinking about shots,” she said. “Where does the camera need to go? What does the performance need to be? What does it need to cut to? What are the elements or the assets that we need to get there? Who has the best skills [and] where could be using AI artists to do that?
	

	“We start with production designers to design what’s happening. We’ll generate 20 shots of something, and 19 are going to be wrong. But those 19 are important. It’s human judgment that you need to know what’s wrong.”

	When pre-visualizing scripts with producers and directors, Sissoko is helping producers and directors not only identify potential problems but also make smart decisions on what needs to be filmed and where money needs to be spent.

	“We collaborate with VFX teams as well,” he said. “They might have something ready in 3D, and they want us to kind of slap the skin on it, give them an overall idea of what the cut might look like.”

	In hybrid production, Sissoko says the challenge today is reducing dependence on what the AI model generates, finding ways to blend the AI with the real footage in seamlessly. “Getting the AI to not only keep the actor’s performance intact but add to it is very tricky,” he said. “That’s one of the things that I work on.”

	In both animated and live-action film contexts, the panelists agreed that greater control in AI film workflow environments is what they’re looking forward to in the coming months. “I need them to obey me more,” Shorthouse said, prompting an amused reaction from the panel and audience. “So if I say, I want this character here in this costume in this environment but just change the eye line, I just want it to just change that not everything else.”

	“Every 90 days there’s a huge improvement – I mean, if you’re going from three-second-generated videos to 15 seconds with more consistency across the board,” said Sissoko, who got into the industry making concept trailers, which he uses as an example. “If you can take a pitch deck, have a conversation with a producer and cut together a trailer that gets the story picked up, you are creating work for a lot of people, you’re helping make someone’s dream come true.”

	Shorthouse’s advice to emerging filmmakers in the room is to hands-on learn the craft. “Know what shots you want, how things work from cameras to lighting to performances, and then experiment with AI,” she said. “And put all your knowledge of filmmaking into the prompts.”

	Sissoko said he tells people who are starting to use AI in filmmaking that learning to write is the most crucial skill. “Before anything, learn how to write stories. [It] will help you with the prompts, as well.”

schema.headline: Kling AI’s TIFF Market Panel Illuminates Tech Challenges and Human-Led Solutions in AI Filmmaking: ‘The Script Is Still the Blueprint’

title: Love Has Everything to Do With It: Darlene Love, Producer Taraji P. Henson and Director Barry Avrich on ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been,’ a Stirring Music Doc Premiering in Toronto
description: The truly legendary singer Darlene Love had her story already lightly sketched out in a 2013 film about backup singers of yore, 2013’s Oscar-winnin
body:
The truly legendary singer Darlene Love had her story already lightly sketched out in a 2013 film about backup singers of yore, 2013’s Oscar-winning “20 Feet From Stardom.” But what Love’s fans — and they are legion — really have hungered for is a movie in which she is less than 10 feet from the camera for the length of a feature film, one devoted solely to her life and career. They are getting it with “Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been,” an illuminating and spirit-lifting doc premiering at the Toronto International Film Festival Sunday night.

	Love’s fame was renewed and in part kept alive by annual performances of her Phil Spector-helmed classic “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home)” on David Letterman’s late-night programs. But music fans with only a cursory knowledge of Love as the original queen of Christmas will relish learning about dozens of classic songs they had no idea she sang lead or backup on. Thankfully, after a period in which her career stalled enough that she became a house cleaner in Beverly Hills, Love was persuaded by Steven Van Zandt to move to New York and rebuild her career there, which led to such heights as a costarring role in the “Lethal Weapon” movies and a starring role on Broadway in “Hairspray,” where her bravura ballad each night was the civil rights-themed anthem “I Know Where I’m Going,” a key lyric from which gives this new documentary its name.

	Director Barry Avrich has spent two years on the project, and was joined in it by celebrity superfan-turned-producer Taraji P. Henson, whose production company, TPH Entertainment, brought it to the finish line. The doc has its enjoyable share of talking heads, but some of its most stirring scenes are performances shot especially for the movie in a New York studio with Love being backed by a Paul Shaffer-led band, potent as ever in her 80s. Variety spoke with Love, Avrich and Henson in the days leading up to the Toronto premiere, and we also have this exclusive first look at the movie’s trailer.



	A lot of people have gotten a taste of Darlene’s story before, but it’s not so many who have been given a chance to really dig in. What was the impetus for making this happen and how did everyone come to be involved?

	Barry Avrich: For me, Darlene Love is one of these people that just kept entering my life in different times. In 2002, I went to see “Standing in the Shadows of Motown,” the film about the Funk Brothers, at the Toronto Film Festival, and I sat there amazed at the cadence of the film and how the audience would applaud after each performance, and how incredible this unknown entity was in the back line of Motown. I said, “I want to make a movie like that one day.” Then I started to talk to Doug Blush, the Academy Award-winning editor, about editing a film for me in the art world. I asked him what he was working on, and he told me about “Twenty Feet From Stardom,” and he said, “You know, when this comes out, have a look at Darlene Love.” And I said, “My God, I’ve never forgotten about her.” Going back before that, I had met with Don Kirshner and Phil Spector in Las Vegas about a television show concept, and Phil had brought up Darlene, and so her name just kept coming back to me.


	Then as I started to do my research on Darlene Love before even approaching her, what would amaze me as the through line in this movie is, she’s gotta be probably one of the nicest people in show business, number one. Number two is this community that surrounded her with love and wanted to make sure that she had a life and a career, and that she never gave up. Certainly Darlene never gave up. There were moments, but this talent continued forever. That’s when I approached her and said, “I have an idea,” and talked about the arc of her story, and we got moving pretty quickly.



	How long have you been working on it now?

	Avrich: Two years, which is longer than usual, but we have such a big cast. Plus, we wanted to bring Darlene into the recording studio, into Power Station in New York, and convince her to do some numbers. I think the audience needed to see that this incredible icon, this person who I believe is the alchemy of the greatest, today and yesterday and forever, still has the performance chops. And so that recording session, along with all of the other stuff we planned to do, the sessions with her and her family and the other people in the film… Then, as we were making the film, that’s when I approached Taraji. And given her love of the music industry and love of performance, she became the number one person for me that I said, “I want to tell this story, and can we do this together?” That became a bit of the dream team for me here.

	Taraji P. Henson: I’ll tap in there. For me it was a no-brainer. I’m very passionate about stories about… let’s call them hidden figures, you know? Pun intended. Darlene’s voice is so recognizable, and it just blew my mind: How can we all know her voice and not know who this woman is? I was compelled to help in any way I could tell this woman’s story, because to not know is like a, a crime. To see her resilience, to see how she never gave up, it’s because of women like her that I exist. I understand being a mother in the industry trying to make your dreams come true and all of the obstacles. I did it. Her name is Darlene Love. My middle name means love in Swahili; Pendameans love. My first name means hope. So it made sense to me. This is a story that is going to inspire so many people, and that is what my production company is about. I’m about: how do you inspire someone through this gift that God gave you? And boy, did God give this queen, Darlene Love, a gift. And I think what’s gonna shock so many people is that her voice is still as powerful today as it was in the ’60s. And just how well Barry put the story together —I was like, “God, seriously, this just fell in my lap like this? Thank you.”



	

					Darlene Love
									Courtesy TIFF
	



	Avrich: I will tell you that the one thing we sent to Taraji was not even the film yet. It was a little sizzle reel we put together, two and a half minutes, to say, “Here’s what we’re thinking the arc of the story is.” The next milestone was this private room in New York City with Taraji and Darlene together. They had seen nothing, and I had a rough cut, and I just wanted to take their temperature. In some 70 films I’ve done, it was one of the greatest moments in my life to watch Darlene’s life through Darlene’s eyes, and Taraji’s, and watch the two of them sit together as these two powerful women and watch this story unfold. I couldn’t take my eyes off of them through that cut.


	Henson: I couldn’t take my eyes off of Darlene. I sat right beside her, and I would look at her, and there were times when they would talk about some of the darkest moments in her life, and she would throw her head back and let out this belly gut laugh. I mean, if they asked me and I’d been through all that, that would be the moment I’d break down and cry and need some tissue.. But I’m telling you, every time, I would look over at her and she would still have that joy on her face watching her story unfold — I’m sure being triggered left and right. I remember asking her when it was over, “These questions, when they got tough, you threw your head back and you laughed. I find that amazing. Where does that come from?” And she said it was from her father. I’ve been telling everybody this story, Ms. Darlene. She said her father always told her to laugh at the devil before the devil can get up in the corner and laugh at you.
	

	I’m glad you brought that up, because I was thinking back on the few times I’ve interviewed Darlene over the years, on the phone, and being struck and captivated by her laugh.

	Henson: Mm-hmm. You’ll never forget that laugh, baby.
	

	Darlene, it makes it seem like you are unusually comfortable on camera, watching you smile and hearing you laugh even when you are being asked to go there in talking about trouble involving family and sons and husbands, as well as all the career stuff that people know more about.

	Darlene Love: The biggest part about me, guys, is my laughter. I have had to learn to laugh through so much, especially in this business. I always said two of the hardest businesses in our world are being an entertainer or a preacher, because they have to put up with people. And in our churches there’s different, everybody got their own opinion about everything from Jesus to the devil. And they express it not just to me, but they expressed a lot of things to my (pastor) father as one of the members of his church: “How could you allow your daughter to sing that devil’s music?” And then he would go, “What devil’s music are you talking about? God created music. And why were you watching (her on television)? If you had never been watching it, you would never seen her. So it’s OK for you to watch it but not for her to do it?” So those are things I could really laugh about. I’ve had to always dig down into my spiritual beliefs from the time I started singing “Da Doo Ron Ron” [which was credited to the Crystals but actually sung by Love] up till today, because that’s the only glue that holds me together.

	When I think about Taraji, I thought she was a dream, like somebody you would never get to meet, because I’ve always admired her. You can tell who she is in her movies. People may not even like the movie, but there is something in you, Taraji, a spark when you play a role. You come out, too, you know what I’m saying? So getting her to be part of this movie was life-opening to me. It was like, “What a wonderful thing is this, Lord. Lord, thank you for bringing her to me.” Because I was always a person that helped people. You know, “Can you sing this song for me? Can you make this audition?” There’s so many people in this film I’ve done that for, and I got joy in doing all those things, whether it was making the Beach Boys records, or Jan and Dean… I had fun. It growed me into this business. I worked for Dionne Warwick as a background singer for 10 years, and we never had a cross word, because I know when to be the employee and when to be the friend, and they don’t get confused. And I still have those same friends in my life, which makes me thrilled, to see that I can go to these people and say, “Can you be in this film… will you?” “Are you kidding? When?” That’s the other part of this business. It will pay off. If you hang in there and you know what you’re doing and you know where you’re trying to go, those people will stick with you.

	And then there’s this film, where people say, “I can’t believe I don’t know who you are, but I know your voice.” That’s all right. It’s coming.

	Henson: Yes, and I wanted to be a part of the “it’s coming.” The world needs to know. I was blown away by how many songs this woman’s voice has been a part of. That’s gonna blow peoeple away. I can’t wait to watch it with an audience. I can’t wait. I’ve got goosebumps right now.

	Avrich: I can’t wait to be with Darlene and Taraji again in this 1,400-seat theater when she lets out a performance and lets out a note. I think people are gonna miss dialogue because it’s just gonna be these incredible applause breaks of just, “Holy, whoa.”
	

	There is one moment where I imagine there might actually be a lot of booing in the theater.

	Henson: Oh, yeah!

	And it’s when there is a clip of Phil Spector being interviewed later in his life, and he says something obviously no sane person would say out loud on camera, even if you thought it: that all the singers he worked with, including Darlene, were interchangeable. It’s easy to imagine boos breaking out at that moment…
	

	Henson: I did it in the screening. I booedin the screening, and Darlene let out that laugh again. You know, she went, “Ah-ha-ha.” I cursed that day.

	Love: While we were sitting together, Taraji goes, “She needs to get everything,” and she made this face like she was talking to him face to face. That was the funniest thing to me.

	Henson: Mm, mm, mm, mm. I want to see this woman get every flower, every rose petal, every leaf from the plant that she deserves. I want her to get all the gold, all the silver, everything. She deserves it.



	

					Darlene Love
									Courtesy TIFF
	



	To talk for a minute about the guest interviewees in the film, you don’t have a million of them, but they’re all very valuable. Who was most necessary in providing either context or stories of friendship?

	Avrich: It’s choreography. Everybody played a different role in Darlene’s life at a different time, and so I wanted that, whether it was David Letterman or Dionne Warwick or Cher or Marc Shaiman. I mean, they’re all there for a specific moment and not just a “Hey, she’s great” jukebox. For me, one of the most exciting parts of the film in terms of those interviews, aside from Darlene, was Steven Van Zandt, to talk about the musicology and technique of Darlene’s voice, and what were some of the obstacles for her in the business, as well as just her sheer range. When he does an analysis of “River Deep, Mountain High,” Darlene [who was originally slated by Spector to record the song] versus Tina Turner, we’re going to school. We edited note by note, almost, to show that, and I think that was one of the most exciting interviews. I probably spent the most time with him, aside from my sessions with Darlene, because he is an artist and understands composition and performance, so that was a big one for me.
	

	And the others… The interview with Dionne minutes before going on stage was iconic for me, and you understood the the love between two people that went back decades and decades and decades. And then from the Springsteen perspective, we spent a fair bit of time with him in terms of, again, to Taraji’s point, he was like, “I’m gonna do everything I can for Darlene because she deserves everything… What do we have to do here to make sure that this icon is an icon?” So just that love, pardon the pun intended, was just so much a currency of the film.

	Darlene, when you finally started to get your due and have a comeback, it was long overdue. And yet, as the film establishes, your comeback has been going on for about 45 years now…

	Love: Right. It has been about 40 years, you’re absolutely right.

	Which is refreshing to think about, because we all know some people only get it at the end of their life, and after. But there was a moment in the early ’80s when people started to realize who Darlene Love was, so you’ve had a while to get used to those accolades. And obviously you’ve been in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame for a while now. But getting this kind of feature-length film treatment is still a milestone. Were you able to enjoy being the subject of it and think, yes, I deserve this?

	Love: You know, when you reach certain heights, every time I reach one, I would say, “Well, thank you, God. Thank you, thank you.” But I think the biggest height for me was when I got recognized as a backup singer. As a backup singer, they treated me like I was one of them. I was never treated like a backup singer. And for me to be walk down that aisle at the Academy Awards and receive that award for something I have been doing for years and years and years that I love [she was at the podium when “Twenty Feet From Stardom” won the best documentary Oscar, and sang a bit, a cappella]… Now, to flip it, and now it’s being about just me personally… It’s like Taraji says, “OK, it’s time for her flowers.” It’s time. And you can’t really put a whole lot more on that word than it’s time. That’s really the way I feel about it. This film, I think, immortalizes something forever. Jimmy Jones said to me, “You can’t have a beautiful picture without the negative.” And if this is a life that personifies those words, that’s what it’s been, and we have a beautiful picture here.

schema.headline: Love Has Everything to Do With It: Darlene Love, Producer Taraji P. Henson and Director Barry Avrich on ‘Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been,’ a Stirring Music Doc Premiering in Toronto

title: ‘Diablo’ Animated Series in the Works at Netflix, Blizzard Entertainment
description:
An animated TV series adaptation of Blizzard Entertainment’s popular “Diablo” video game franchise is in development at Netflix.

	“Diablo” is set t
body:
An animated TV series adaptation of Blizzard Entertainment’s popular “Diablo” video game franchise is in development at Netflix.

	“Diablo” is set the dark world of Sanctuary, where humanity is caught in the eternal conflict between the High Heavens and the Burning Hells. 

	Per Blizzard’s official description of the project, “After decades of bringing entire universes to life through our games, we’re partnering with some creative powerhouses to tell even more stories beyond gaming across new screens. A new animated series set in the world of ‘Diablo’ is in development with Netflix. More details will be shared in the future, but this is only the beginning, with even more taking shape across our universes.”
	

	The first “Diablo” game launched in 1996, marking this year as the 30th anniversary of the action-RPG franchise. The most recent “Diablo” game, “Diablo IV,” launched in 2023.


	The “Diablo” TV series development news was announced by Blizzard president Johanna Faries during the opening ceremony of BlizzCon 2026 at the Anaheim Convention Center on Saturday. The two-day fan-festival event, which is the first BlizzCon since Microsoft closed its $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard in 2023, is a celebration of all things Blizzard Entertainment, from “Diablo” to “World of Warcraft” to “Overwatch.”

	“BlizzCon in and of itself represents so much for all of us to be able to shine a light on all the great work going on at Blizzard,” Faries told Variety in an interview ahead of the event. “We have put a lot of thought into this moment, and why now, and how do we continue to capture and build on the momentum we’re experiencing as an organization.”
	

	Variety will be on the ground at BlizzCon Sept. 12-13 and readers can follow along with our coverage of the event here.

schema.headline: ‘Diablo’ Animated Series in the Works at Netflix, Blizzard Entertainment

title: Alan Rickman Brought Kids ‘From the Hospital’ to the ‘Harry Potter’ Set, Says Co-Star Gary Oldman: ‘He Knew How Much It Meant’
description: While Alan Rickman’s legendary “Harry Potter” character, Severus Snape, may have been notoriously hard on the children at Hogwarts, in real life, th
body:
While Alan Rickman’s legendary “Harry Potter” character, Severus Snape, may have been notoriously hard on the children at Hogwarts, in real life, the actor couldn’t have been more different from the pupil-hating professor. 

	In fact, Rickman would “bring in kids every single day” to the sets, said Gary Oldman, who played Sirius Black in the “Harry Potter” films, at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival on Thursday. 
	

	“He would bring them in from a school, he’d bring them in from the hospital, he’d bring friends and their kids in every single day for lunchtimes and things,” Oldman said. “He’d take kids around to tour the sets, and we’d meet them.”


	Oldman noted that Rickman believed it was “the most extraordinary thing, that he was in this world that he got to be in, come in every day, and that he knew how much it meant to these kids. So, he wanted to share it.” He continued to call him “the cheerleader of it”: “He was into it, he was doing it, so he was with it and committed to it,” he said. 

	In a recent interview with EW, the “Darkest Hour” actor also shared that he believes HBO’s forthcoming TV adaptation of the original subject material will be even “more satisfying,” since more of the wizarding world will be able to be covered. 

	“We had to cut a lot [for the ‘Harry Potter’ movies], and still we could only get the films down to, like, three hours,” Oldman told the outlet. “I believe [the HBO series is] gonna do it pretty much word-for-word.” 

	Rickman died on Jan. 14, 2016, following a battle with cancer. The actor starred in films including “Die Hard” and “Truly Madly Deeply,” as well as portraying Snape in all the “Harry Potter” films.

schema.headline: Alan Rickman Brought Kids ‘From the Hospital’ to the ‘Harry Potter’ Set, Says Co-Star Gary Oldman: ‘He Knew How Much It Meant’

title: Drake Reveals ‘Fear of Missing Out’ Teaser, Says Project Is a ‘Not So Short Film’
description:
Drake on Saturday released a teaser for “Fear of Missing Out,” a “not so short film” set for release on Sept. 15.

	Fans have long speculated whethe
body:
Drake on Saturday released a teaser for “Fear of Missing Out,” a “not so short film” set for release on Sept. 15.

	Fans have long speculated whether “Fear of Missing Out” would be an album, a music video or a world tour. With the teaser’s release, Drake revealed that “FOMO” is some sort of film. Drake dropped the teaser on Instagram and wrote in the caption that the project was a “not so short film directed and scored by the family.”
	


	The teaser shows a man, presumably Drake, zooming across a calm ocean in a neon green speedboat. A woman narrator says over the footage, “What if I told you there were two versions of your life? In one, you avoid risk and withhold love. You feel like you’ve gone missing from yourself. You look for something you can’t find. In the other version of your life, you find it.” The teaser then drops the title card for “Fear of Missing Out,” which Drake revealed on Sept. 3, along with the release date.


	Drake’s last major release came when he dropped the long-rumored “Iceman” album, along with two more surprise records, “Habibti” and “Maid of Honour.” The three albums had a total of 43 songs and featured collaborations from Future, 21 Savage, Sexyy Red, Qendresa, Molly Santana, Central Cee, Popcaan, PartyNextDoor, Loe Shimmy, Iconic Savvy and Stunna Sandy.

	The five-time Grammy winner is no stranger to elaborate rollouts. While promoting “Iceman,” Drake installed a 25-foot-tall ice sculpture in a Toronto parking lot.

schema.headline: Drake Reveals ‘Fear of Missing Out’ Teaser, Says Project Is a ‘Not So Short Film’

title: Fire at Senior Living Facility in Chiles Leaves 16 Dead
description:
Senior Living Facility Fire
                          16 Killed, 10 Hospitalized
body:
Senior Living Facility Fire
                          16 Killed, 10 Hospitalized
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 12, 2026
                            10:23 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A fire that erupted in a senior living facility has left 16 dead ... and only 10 survivors made it out of the blaze alive.
      
    
            The fire -- which is currently under investigation -- broke out at the facility in El Edén, Chile, late Friday night, according to multiple reports.
      
    
            After the blaze was put out by the fire department, they had the somber task of pulling the remains of those who perished from the ruins.
      

            General Miguel Herrera revealed in a statement given to La Tercera that “only 10 people living in the nursing home were evacuated.”
      
    
            The Organized Crime and Homicide team is reportedly working to determine the cause of the fire ... and the Carabineros Criminalistics laboratory is collaborating with the criminal investigation department OS-9 on the investigation, according to the Public Prosecutor's office.
      
    
            The prosecutor told 24 Horas ... "There were about 26 adult people. According to initial investigations, not all were elderly who were in this home. There was one person in charge of them, a nursing assistant, and in that context, for reasons that are being investigated, a fire broke out that [caused] the death of 16 people."

title: Woman Dead After Undergoing 6 Cosmetic Procedures at Once
description:
Brazilian Woman
                          Dead After 8-Hour Surgery, 6 Cosmetic Procedures At Onc
body:
Brazilian Woman
                          Dead After 8-Hour Surgery, 6 Cosmetic Procedures At Once
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 12, 2026
                            7:23 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 12, 2026
                                8:15 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A woman who underwent 6 cosmetic procedures at once during a marathon 8-hour procedure has died ... and now the 51-year-old's sister is demanding answers.
      
    
            Andreia Vieira Gaspar had saved $118K Brazilian Real -- equivalent to $22,918 USD -- over two years to undergo the plastic surgery -- which involved a facelift, blepharoplasty, liposuction and facial fat grafting -- in Goiânia, Brazil.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Andreia, who was living in Spain before the surgery, died in the days after the procedure on August 12 ... G1 reported.
      
    
            Now her sister Djiane Vieira is saying Andreia -- whose dream was to have this surgery -- did not have a pre-procedure consultation ... and that her pre-op tests were done in Spain, not Brazil.
      

            Djiane says that after Andreia's tongue started swelling severely, she tried reaching out to the doctor's medical team ... but her sister says didn't receive the proper care before it was too late.
      
    
            She told G1 ... "My sister is dying. For God’s sake. You answer the phone, but nobody shows up. For God’s sake."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She claims that the local Ankar Hospital did not have an ICU or an emergency ambulance.
      
    
            According to Djiane ... Andreia died in her arms after multiple resuscitation attempts were made.
      
    
            Dr. Lessandro Martins said in a legal statement ... "Out of respect for medical confidentiality — which persists even after death, as mandated by the Medical Code of Ethics — no interviews will be granted, nor will comments be made regarding clinical data... The doctor trusts that the investigation will demonstrate the correctness of the care provided."
      
    
            Meanwhile, a lawyer representing Ankar Hospital says Andreia "received immediate emergency care" and "necessary measures were taken" to treat her.
